chapter_theme: Noble birth (குடிப்பிறப்பு) shows in conduct that holds through poverty: the well-born keep their principles, courtesy and generosity when they have nothing, while the low-born fail to do good even when they can. The chapter treats these qualities as belonging to birth.
structure_note: Most quatrains pair the well-born with an image of something that keeps its nature in distress: the hungry lion (141), the ruined mansion with a dry corner (147), the moon half-swallowed by the serpent (148), the dry river that yields water when dug (150). 142, 145, 146 and 149 make the contrast with others explicit.

141.reading: Even when their clothes are in rags and their bodies wasted, the well-born do not fall from their principles; would a lion, however hard pressed, chew creeping grass?
141.nuance: The lion is chosen because grass is not merely beneath it but against its nature, so the verse makes principle a matter of what one is. Mudaliar records a variant reading, வரிமா, which would make the animal a tiger.

142.reading: Fullness of character, gentleness and good conduct belong only to those born of a family that touches the sky; they do not come to others even when they gain great wealth, lord of the hills where clouds creep.
142.nuance: The point is aimed at wealth: money cannot buy these qualities. Mudaliar glosses சாயல் as mildness, restraint in mind, word and body, and notes that some take it as restraint from blame and sin.

143.reading: Rising from one's seat, going out to meet, seeing a guest off, and the like are what the well-born have taken as unfailing conduct; they are not to be thought of as one with the base.
143.nuance: Only Shanmuganar's commentary is aligned here, and the readings of விடுப்ப ஒழிதல் (as seeing off) and of whom the courtesies are for (elders who visit) are his.

144.reading: If the well-born do good, it is called their nature; if they do evil, it becomes blame spread by many; what then does a person gain from the all-knowing high birth that falls to them?

positions.position: The closing question is ironic: high birth brings no gain of its own, since good is credited to birth and evil is loudly blamed.
positions.quote: எல்லாம் உணர்ந்த உயர்குடியில் பிறந்ததால் அவருக்குச் சொந்த நன்மை என்னவோ?

144.nuance: Pope reads the same question the other way, as praise: what greater good can come to anyone than high birth? So the two readings reach opposite conclusions. Mudaliar's commentary isn't aligned for this quatrain, so this can't be recorded as a contest between commentators.

145.reading: Fear of being unlearned, fear of base work, fear of a slip in speech, and fear of not giving to those who ask: those born of an undistinguished family who lack all these are like wood.
145.nuance: These fears are presented as marks of good birth, a moral sensitivity. The third fear is read two ways: Pope takes it as dread of a careless word, and Shanmuganar as the dismay of being unable to speak in an assembly of the good.

146.reading: Good company, sweet speech, giving, and goodness of mind are all found only among the well-born, lord of the cool shore of the roaring sea where great gems gleam with pearls.
146.nuance: The claim is exclusive: these qualities are found only among the well-born, not merely more often.

147.reading: A great house whose woodwork has decayed and which white ants have overrun still keeps one corner where the rain does not fall; so even when hardship presses, the well-born do what is theirs to do.
147.nuance: The image does not claim the house is intact, only that some shelter remains; the well-born, too, can do less but not nothing.

148.reading: Like the moon that lights the wide fair earth with one side while the serpent holds the other, the well-born do not slacken in serving others even when poverty stands squarely before them.
148.nuance: The serpent is the eclipse, as Shanmuganar notes. The last line shares its words, ஒப்புரவிற்கு ஒல்கார், with Kural 218.

149.reading: What the well-born do even when they cannot, the small will not do even when they can; an antelope may bear a saddle, but it cannot do battle like a leaping horse.
149.nuance: The saddle is outward equipment, so the verse says that giving the small the means does not give them the nature.

150.reading: Even when they have nothing at all, the well-born are a prop to those who come to them in need, as a wide river, when dried up, yields clear water at once if you dig its bed.
150.nuance: The river image implies that the means of giving is still there below the surface; the well-born have to be dug for, not asked from.

links.note: Both use an animal that will not go against its nature in extremity: the yak that dies when it loses a hair, and the lion that will not eat grass. The Kural speaks of honour, the Naladiyar of the principles of the well-born.

Both name three qualities the well-born never lose. The Kural's are conduct, truthfulness and shame; the Naladiyar's are fullness of character, gentleness and conduct, and it adds that wealth cannot buy them.
Both say a fault in the well-born is seen by everyone, the Kural like the spot on the moon and the Naladiyar as blame spread by many.
Both call people who lack a human moral quality trees or wood: in the Kural those without courtesy, however sharp, and in the Naladiyar the low-born who lack the four fears.
Both say a moral fear or shame is found naturally only in the well-born.
Both list four qualities of a good lineage, and both include giving and sweet speech.

146 says that good company, sweet speech, giving and goodness of mind are found only among the well-born. 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from the deeds one does. The two disagree about whether excellence follows birth or deeds. The tension holds if 972's distinction means worth of character, as Pope and Kalaignar take it, and if 146's qualities belong to that worth.
219 says that, for a good man, poverty is being unable to do what should be done. 147 says the well-born still do it even in hardship, so for them poverty in that sense never fully arrives.
The two share the phrase ஒப்புரவிற்கு ஒல்கார்: those who know their duty, or the well-born, do not slacken in serving others when they lack the means. The Naladiyar adds the half-eclipsed moon.
Both say the base do not give even when they could: in the Kural they won't shake off their wet hands for anyone but those who would break their jaws.
Both say that the well-born keep their generous nature when their means have shrunk.

source_issues: 141: Shanmuganar's field ends with the Tamil text and Shanmuganar's commentary for 142, and 142 has no Shanmuganar commentary of its own. Shanmuganar's verse numbers for 141 and 146 read 41 and 46.
142: the Tamil text is corrupted in இநவ்முன்றும் (probably இவைமூன்றும்) and வேற்ப (probably வெற்ப).
143: Pope's translation and Mudaliar's commentary are not aligned.
144 to 148: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned.
150: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.
